title: Maternal experience with predation risk enhances antipredator behavior of their offspring in a wolf spider
content:
Abstract
There is widespread evidence that parental experience with predators can influence offspring in ways that enhance survival when facing those same threats. Such transgenerational effects (TGEs) can shape morphology, life history, development, and behavior. Behavior is particularly intriguing because it is highly flexible and can be adjusted by an individual's own experience, potentially reducing the role of parental influence. We investigated maternal effects on antipredator behavior in the small wolf spider Pardosa milvina, which shows strong immediate responses to chemotactile cues from its intraguild predator, Tigrosa helluo. In the laboratory, we exposed immature females to predator cues. When they reached adulthood, we mated them with predator-naïve males, and documented the behavior of their offspring in their third-instar and a separate group as adults. Both immatures and adults reduced foraging in response to immediate predator cues, but maternal exposure had no additional effect on this trait. Immature offspring of exposed mothers lowered their activity, a response previously shown to reduce predation by T. helluo, though this effect was not evident in adults. When enclosed with a predator, immature offspring of exposed mothers required more effort to subdue, and adult offspring of exposed mothers avoided attack longer and survived longer than controls. These findings indicate that TGEs manifest differently in immatures as compared to adults but ultimately enhance offspring survival in predator interactions throughout all life stages.
